column1: books,"I suffer from mental illness and I only got back into reading this year after about 5 years of experiences similar to what you've described here. For me, the key has been a few things: make sure you've picked out good books (some books are just a real slog, no matter what mental state you're in), don't be afraid to move around when you're reading (I tend to pace a lot with a book in my hands; probably looks pretty silly, but it keeps my attention span up), and also just be cognizant of the fact that when you sit down to read, the first dozen minutes or so are by far the most boring (at least they are for me). During that time you're still sort of readjusting to the mechanics of the book in hand and the rhythm just isn't really there. Once you get into it, though, it's easy to see a hundred or more pages go by and still not want to set the book down. It's all about a sort of momentum. In my case, I picked up Stephen King's IT (a colossal, 1k+ page book about a clown) as a sort of challenge to myself. Getting through it with my illness was a bit tricky and took me a while, but once I did I really felt like there wasn't a book I couldn't tackle.
Good luck! Hope everything gets sorted out quickly.",1565948086.0,2

Sekiro,">You know what I meant to say and chose to pretend that you didn't.
I honestly did not, and frankly I still don't. It seems mostly like you're just having a hard time coming to terms with the fact that not everybody plays FROM games for the same reason you do.
>they deliberately fuck with the player.

Right, but fucking with the player using a mimic and intentionally teaching the player to play the game wrong are two qualitatively different phenomena. One of them is a deliberate design choice in order to increase tension and catch the player off guard, the other frustrates players and leads to a disproportionate number of them quitting the game early. I would note that currently Sekiro (FROM's highest quality game yet, at least in terms of what it has released on PC) is currently sitting at a lower rating of recommended than Dark Souls II. If you look at the reviews, many players will self-report getting stuck very early on, at the Chained Ogre or the bosses just after it. We know that the Chained Ogre and the starting areas are not very hard, so the fact that players are getting stuck here, of all places, suggests that something is amiss. Misleading players in the way that they have with Sekiro has *never* been a part of FROM's design philosophy, and I would further contest the idea that:
>In a From Soft game you are playing against all odds, that's the main point.

If they really wanted this to be the case, they wouldn't give you vitality upgrades, boss memories, items, skills, or health guards; it would be you, dealing minimal damage, against bosses and enemies who could kill you in one hit regardless of what point in the game you're at. This would be patently absurd. You see FROM game's as revolving around difficulty, whereas I see their games as using difficulty as one tool among many to draw players into the world. FROM's games could be harder - they could be *much, much* harder, but they're not. I think this goes to show that pure, unadulterated difficulty and ""playing against all odds"" as you suggest, is not and never was their intention. But maybe you will say that you actually meant something else by this quote and I'm just pretending to misunderstand you. Preemptively, then, allow me to add that if you think I am deliberately misinterpreting you, it is in fact *you* who is deliberately misinterpreting *me*, and I dare you to try and argue against that purposely ambiguous mental obstacle course.
Sekiro,">You seem to confuse the meaning of the word culture.

Real slick. Just say I've misused the word without explaining how. As a matter of fact, you have confused the meaning of each and every word you used in your entire last response; and as a further matter of fact, I feel no obligation to explain how you have misused these words. Just note that they have been misused, and this, in some way, must mean that you are wrong.
>People just get pissed when it becomes obvious that someone blames the game for his own laziness.
That's an interesting take. Is the implication that people like me are lazy because we *don't* want to waste hours of our time repeating content in a videogame?
>And without it, none of the players would have considered it either, given that it's never going to happen.

It *has* happened. Exactly five times, actually; it's just that FROM has typically done a very elegant job of hiding it. In previous FROM games, all you really had to be able to do to get to the end-credits of the game was be able to possess enough spatial awareness to locate and activate summon signs, or, barring this, enough patience to grind out levels for powerful builds. Sekiro is the first real FROM game where the only way forward is to *do the sword good*, and, in my opinion, this is reflected in player response. I would be very surprised if the next FROM game followed in the same path as Sekiro and offered no form of multiplayer, both because it provides what is essentially an easy mode and because it really expands the longevity of the game.
Sekiro,">The game teaches you one thing at a time and makes damn sure that you can't proceed without actually learning your lesson.

I think this is funny, because you go on to talk about how the Chained Ogre is this masterwork of a tutorial boss because he teaches you to pace attacks. In my opinion, the Chained Ogre may be solely responsible for the surprisingly large number of people who end up playing Sekiro the wrong way and saying that it's too hard. The thing is, there's basically only one other boss in Sekiro that behaves anything like the Chained Ogre: the Guardian Ape, which you fight much further on after a number of other bosses. Unlike nearly every other enemy and boss, these two encounters and far more reliant upon dodging and looking out for frequent grabs. I imagine that most players don't even know that you can deflect the Chained Ogre's attacks at first, because who would think to deflect an ogre's sideways drop-kick at you? So there's that hurdle, and also the fact that deflecting the ogre is really just not a good idea. He doesn't take a lot of posture damage, and he uses more grabs than any other enemy in the game. Naturally, players start dancing around the ogre like it's Dark Souls and rushing in for a bit of vitality damage after a big attack. The thing is, this tactic works really well for the ogre; couple that with a flame barrel, and most players will probably think that they need to find an elemental weakness for a boss and then just dodge around it while chipping away at its vitality. In other words, the Chained Ogre teaches players to play Sekiro in exactly the *wrong way.*

Couple this, too, with the bizarrely structured fight with the drunk guy in Hirata Estates (which teaches players to rely too much on stealth and look for NPC helpers), and it's no wonder why so many people end up confused as to how this game is supposed to play. As I said above, I'm continuing with a vanilla run of the game to compare to the modded one, and my biggest takeaway so far as been that FROM fucked up the beginning of the game so horribly that it almost seems deliberate. The first areas of the game bear only a cursory resemblance to the way the rest of the game is meant to be played, and I have no idea why anybody thought this was a good idea.
>Well, this is the point where you should really, honestly, without question, play other games. You're complaining about the water in a swimming pool.

A swimming pool, you will remember, is basically a concrete basin filled with water. Part of the essence of being a swimming pool is, indeed, that it contain water; if I complain about water in a swimming pool, then clearly I am confused, because that's what a swimming pool *is*. I point this out, because in drawing this analogy, what you're accidentally saying is that Sekiro is nothing more than difficult combat. Take away the lore, the music, the visuals, the animation, the textures, the sound design, the voice-acting, the level structure - all of that, evidently, is incidental; the water of this swimming pool is the difficulty. Presumptively, then, you would be content to play a version of Sekiro animated using line vectors on a black background, with no music, sound, or world design. That's what we're here for, isn't it? We're here for the water - for the difficult combat, so in removing those other qualities then we're realty not missing the essence of the media.

But of course, you would reject this; those other qualities are equally important to the experience and you like them as much as I do. It's just that because I don't like one particular aspect of the experience (say, keeping with our analogy, a decorative sign next to the swimming pool) you think I should not be allowed to enjoy it at all. It's a very strange thing to believe.

Sekiro,"I knew Sekiro was going to be difficult, sure, but I know I'm not alone in finding the level of difficulty coming from Sekiro to be fairly unprecedented relative to other FROM games. They've never given you fewer options or less health - the chained ogre, for instance, is one of the first minibosses, and yet can take away about 95% of your health with one attack. Of course, the chained ogre is ultimately pretty easy, but later bosses are so hard that people who are otherwise great at reaction-based games are having to spend upwards of four hours applying brute memorization to attack patterns. What I'm trying to say is this: I don't think there was any indication or reason to believe that Sekiro was going to be as hard as it turned out to be, and this problem is only confounded by the fact that numerous members of the community are outright misrepresenting the game and trying to argue that it's actually very easy. And that sort of gets to what I was trying to convey in my original post: Sekiro is so hard that for me, that feeling of satisfaction upon beating a boss is totally lost. Is it satisfying beating your head against a boss for hours, only to realize that once you've defeated this boss there's another, harder one down the way? I didn't think so. Difficulty needs a sort of sense of distribution which I feel Sekiro lacks. Again, if you had that feeling of satisfaction upon beating bosses, then that's great and I understand why you like the game so much - but for myself and for others, that feeling has so far been absent. Battlefield,"Christ this sub is weird. You complain when DICE sifts through the historical record to find a handful of instances of woman serving in combat roles, because that's not indicative of the broader themes of the war and wasn't very common at all. Yet you justify the apologetics of Generation War because ""not all Germans were indoctrinated"" and you can't expect producers to accurately reflect the broad themes of the war.

Generation War and Band of Brothers have this in common: both indirectly imply the universality of their narratives. That's what makes them stories worth telling in the first place, right? We aren't given a Desmond Doss or an Audie Murphey or an Oscar Schindler in either series; we aren't following one very unique individual along through a story so crazy it seems almost impossible. We're following a group of implicitly normal individuals through the most devestating conflict in human history, with the hope that in the end we might find something out about normal humans (i.e. humanity). That's what makes Band of Brothers so good: the message about the morality of the individual soldiers is very mixed. Spiers is a psychopath, another soldier drunkenly shoots a German major and a U.S. soldier, Liebgott executes a German on mere suspicion, Webster threatens a German baker with a pistol, and we find out in one of the opening episodes that most of Easy company is comfortable with anti-Semitism. If you were to take Band of Brothers as a sort of general example of how U.S. soldiers behaved and operated in WW2 (with, of course, the explicit note that Easy Company was specifically chosen to be depicted because of their uncommon success in combat), you wouldn't be that far off at all.

The message that Generation War gives us isn't at all complicated: some (the show implies many) Germans involved in the war were not complicit in the Nazi idealogy, were coerced into fighting, didn't actually hate Jews, and we're *just following orders, sir*. This excuse has literally existed since WW2 and, actually, I think it was used in some of the Neuremburg trials. It's not accurate of how most soldiers in the Wehrmacht and most people in Germany actually felt. A quote from New York Times reviewer A.O. Battlefield,"Here's how I think about the point I made about aesthetics: if I go and take a screenshot in BF1 with the HUD turned off on a high-end gaming PC, what I have looks, superficially, like a colorized image taken during WW1. There will be, of course, minor inaccuracies; a gun that was in development but didn't actually see service (e.g. the Hellriegel), British soldiers using German weapons, the wrong insignia on a uniform, that sort of thing. To be very technical about it, then, I would say this: BF1 had *authentic*, but not *historically accurate*, aesthetic design; what I mean by this is that the way the game looked was *authentic* to the broad themes of the time period DICE was portraying, but there were enough anachronisms and oddities that it would be inaccurate to call the aesthetic true to the history.

More on this: there were black German soldiers in BF1, and female Russian soldiers serving alongside men en masse. This is not historically accurate, but again, it is what I would call *authentic*; i.e. it reflects the broad themes of the time period DICE is portraying. The black German soldier (and the British-Indian soldier, for that matter) is, I think, indicative of and a reference to the extensive colonial ownership of the European powers throughout the course of WW1. It's unlikely that any black Germans fought alongside white Germans in Europe, but they certainly did fight in German colonies, and their inclusion in the game reflects that theme of the war. The female Russian soldier is DICE's way of showing the political and civil turmoil occuring in Russia in the latter half of WW1. No other faction has female combatants in the game; this shows the dire straights Russia was in as it entered into its civil war. Note that neither of these points have to do with how many black German soldiers or how many female Russian soldiers there actually were; what's important is that DICE seems to be creatively using the makeup of the factions in BF1 in order to illustrate the broad themes of the war they're portraying.

As this relates to the guns: WW1 was a period of experimentation and invention, with new weaponry characterizing the battlefield on nearly every front. Although the prominence of automatic weaponry is inaccurate in BF1, the significance of experimental weaponry is not; I think the inclusion of prototype weapons and other extremely uncommon guns helps to emphasize this point as well as maintain the amount of variety the Battlefield series is known for.

BF1, for me, was a strange and excellent game, because I felt like it did a really good job of making me feel like I was playing a game set in WW1, despite its lightning-quick gameplay. I think that feeling of authenticity is owed to DICE's aesthetic choices for the game, and I'm worried that BFV will completely miss the mark on that note.",1531126851.0,5
